walkthroughs.body_html: A white dwarf has no fusion — it is held up by electron degeneracy pressure, a quantum effect from the Pauli exclusion principle. It is roughly Earth-sized but as massive as the Sun.
Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar (1930) showed that white dwarfs cannot exceed about 1.4 solar masses. Above this, electron pressure fails and the object collapses to a neutron star or detonates.
A white dwarf accreting from a companion can reach the Chandrasekhar limit and ignite carbon explosively — a Type Ia supernova, used as a standard candle to measure cosmic distances.
